title: Budapest Gambit | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: 1681 with the black pieces. Against d4 we develop the knight and get ready for something adventurous.
In a celebratory mood, so we roll out the Budapest Gambit — an underrated, rarely-seen sideline. A great second string once you're around 1700: not bad, a little offbeat, and one you know well.
teaches: Keep an offbeat sideline you know well alongside your main opening

moves.spoken: We toss the e5-pawn onto the board and hope he grabs it. Players in this range are often uneasy facing these second-tier openings, which works in our favor.
He pushes d5 instead of taking — not a great try. It hands us exactly what we want, because advancing that pawn gives up control of the c5-square.
teaches: Advancing a pawn concedes the square beside it

moves.spoken: So we make a natural developing move that also pounces on that hole: the bishop to c5, a lovely nook, with d6 to follow and later c6 to chip at his center.
teaches: Occupy the square your opponent just weakened

moves.spoken: We anchor the bishop with d6 and open the other bishop's diagonal. The position's equal — he's not worse, but he's posing us no problems. Note Bg5 here would be a tactical blunder to Bxf2+.

He plays e4, and this is already dubious: it weakens the d4-square as a future knight outpost, fully opens the diagonal for our bishop pressuring f2, and takes away his own e3 to relieve that pressure.
teaches: e4 here weakens d4 and bares the a7-g1 diagonal

moves.spoken: The move that leaps out is Ng4 — superficial-looking, but genuinely hard to meet. It piles onto f2, and his only defense is an awkward one.
teaches: Hunt the f2 weak point with ...Ng4

moves.spoken: He's forced into the ugly knight to h3. A rule for these d4 positions: the moment that knight leaves f6, think about pushing the f-pawn to f5 to blast open the f-file.
teaches: When the knight leaves f6, consider ...f5 to open the f-file

moves.spoken: But first the ideal setup — we want a rook on f8 backing the f-pawn before we push f5, so we simply castle and complete development.
teaches: Prepare ...f5 by first placing a rook on f8

moves.spoken: On the recap: his f3 could have been met by the strong positional knight to e3, forking into his camp and forcing a decision.
After knight to e3 he essentially has to give up his bishop for it.
And now his structure is grim — our dark-squared bishop is unopposed, raking both long diagonals and dominating a fistful of key squares. A miserable position for White.
teaches: An unopposed bishop that controls both diagonals is a lasting edge

moves.spoken: Later we chose the calm, positional path — knight to d7, connecting the rooks — and his hurried bishop grab actually dropped the exchange. Being patient with a quiet improving move often gets rewarded.
teaches: A patient improving move often provokes the blunder
